explanation: This pole fires retrospectively on the abstract, relational vocabulary of learned expository prose: the (mostly Latinate) nouns, adjectives and stative verbs that state a property, a degree, a relation or an existence instead of naming a concrete thing or a specific action - e.g. existence, absence, tendency, occurrence, prevalence, incidence, severity, significance, importance, capacity, validity, reliability, status, association, relationship; significant, apparent, unclear, substantial, considerable, marginal, negligible, consistent, essential, immune, respiratory; depend, correlate, vary, tend, occur, persist, enable, allow, increase - usually as a burst across the predicate ('increases greatly', 'was statistically significant'). It stays at baseline on concrete objects and substances, proper names and titles, numbers and enumerations, agentive action verbs and their event nominalizations (measured/measurement, obtained, installed/installation, constructed/construction, purchased/purchase), on bare comparatives with no such predicate ('considerably longer'), and throughout informal narrative, dialogue and product/consumer prose.
